title: If He took the ten
hook: what could the ungrateful say if the ten were taken too

segments.voice: Yesterday, das basatoo: ten gifts put behind the back, and trust thrown away over the one. Your line was ten given, one held back. Today the same stanza asks a sharp question. Day four hundred fifty-six.

Back to the birthday table. The child is still sulking over the eleventh present. Now take the whole table away. Not ten and a missing one. Nothing. No cake, no wrapping paper, no party. What would there be to complain about then? Who would there be to complain to? It's a question that stops a sulk in its tracks, and it isn't asked to frighten anyone. It's asked to turn the head around. Guru Arjan asks it in the very next line of the stanza, and then, surprisingly, he doesn't leave us standing in front of the empty table.
screen: `NOW THE TABLE IS EMPTY.` → `WHO WOULD YOU COMPLAIN TO?` → `A QUESTION THAT TURNS THE HEAD.`

segments.voice: The line goes: ek bhee na dei, das bhee hir lei. If He gave not even the one, and took back the ten as well. Then: tau moorhaa kahu kahaa karei. Then tell me, what could the fool do? Moorhaa is a blunt word: the foolish one, the one not thinking. The answer is in the silence after the question. Nothing. There's no court to appeal to, no account to draw on. Everything on the table came from the same hands. So the stanza goes on: jis thaakur sio naahee chaaraa. With the Master before whom we have no leverage, no say. Taa kau keejai sad namaskaaraa: to Him, bow, always. That could sound like fear. Bow, because you have no choice. But listen to the next line, because it changes the whole stanza. Jaa kai man laagaa prabh meethaa: in whose mind God has come to taste sweet. Sarab sookh taahoo man voothaa: every comfort comes to live in that mind. Meethaa is the word for sweet, the taste of sugar on the tongue. So the sum turns into something else. The person who sees the ten and thanks for them isn't cornered into bowing. They've started to love the Giver. And gratitude, for them, stops being a duty and becomes a taste. That's the move: from the empty table, to the full one, to the hands that set it.
screen: `IF HE TOOK THE TEN AS WELL.` · `WHAT COULD THE FOOL DO?` · `BOW TO THE MASTER, ALWAYS.` · `MEETHAA: GOD TASTES SWEET.` · then, large: `THANK FOR THE TEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: be grateful for one small thing. Not the big ones. Something tiny. The warmth of the cup in your hand. A sock without a hole. The light coming in from one window. Pick one, and stay with it. Notice it as if, for a moment, it had been taken away and then handed back. If you pray, you can thank the Giver for it in your own way. If you don't, just let yourself be glad of it, slowly, the way you'd let something sweet sit on your tongue. The bell holds the time.
Meethaa, sweet. Ek bhee na dei, das bhee hir lei: if not even one were given, and the ten taken too, what could anyone do?
Your line: thank for the ten. Today, before you name what's missing, name one thing on the table, out loud or in your head. Day four hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs read this stanza in Sukhmani Sahib, and Sikh teaching treats gratitude to Waheguru as part of everyday remembrance rather than a separate ritual.

what it means: it's a question that turns the head from the missing one to the ten given.
